Join Press Pass from PBS News Democrats Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Amy Acton in Ohio, Rod Sand in Iowa and Gina Hinojosa in Texas won races for governor, flipping GOP-held offices. While Trump urged voters to pretend he was on the ballot, most appear to blame his administration for high costs and want Congress to impose more checks on him, according to The AP Voter Poll. Trump tried to shift the blame away from himself during a Fox News interview that aired early Wednesday, saying Democrats \"did a good job\" in their campaigns and blaming GOP candidates for losses. Here's the latest. 1:31 a.m. EST Democrats win the U.S. House and take unified control of Congress Democrats have won control of the U.S. House in addition to the U.S. Senate, delivering a shockingly decisive rebuke of Republican governance in Washington and ushering in a new era of congressional resistance to Trump. The midterm elections Tuesday channeled voters' deep frustrations over high prices, the Iran war and concerns over government corruption. Democrats routed their rivals across the map, from Texas to Iowa to New Hampshire, including states Trump won by double digits just two years ago. Democratic control will profoundly reshape Trump's final two years in office and likely hamstring his agenda. 1:09 a.m. EST Democrat Troy Jackson wins election to U.S. Senate from Maine Incumbent Sen. Susan Collins conceded earlier to Jackson, ending her run for a sixth term. Democrats considered defeating Collins as key to winning control of the U.S. Senate, and she was one of Republicans' most threatened incumbents this year. Jackson, a former state legislative leader, replaced Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee after Platner dropped out while facing an allegation of sexual assault, which he denied. Sen.-elect Josh Turek says Iowa loves an underdog Turek, a Democrat who flipped Iowa's Republican-held Senate seat, celebrated the win that seemed far-fetched in the state Trump won by 13 percentage points just two years ago. \"They told me it was impossible to win this Senate race, but tonight, Iowa, we have once again proved that the impossible is possible,\" Turek said. Turek will replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst and is among the seat-flipping Democrats ushering in a new majority in the chamber. Turek, who campaigned on rooting out corruption, said he'd be accountable to all Iowans. \"My political North Star has always been about what is best for the people, not about party,\" he said. California defeats voter identification requirements A proposal to enhance California's voter identification requirements had been placed on the ballot after a conservative group gathered thousands of petition signatures. But voters in the Democratic-led state rejected the proposed constitutional amendment Tuesday. Opponents campaigned against it by linking the measure to Trump, who's advocated unsuccessfully for a voter photo ID requirement at the national level. The California measure would have required a government-issued ID to vote in person or the last four digits of that identification number to vote by mail in California. The vast majority of California's ballots are cast by mail. 'We just took back Texas,' Talarico tells crowd after victory That line made the crowd shout with joy, but to Talarico it wasn't about a party victory — even as Democrats tout his Senate win in the Republican state. \"We are tired of being told to hate each other,\" he told a crowd, who yelled in agreement. \"We didn't win this race by alienating our neighbors or shaming our neighbors.\" His campaign, he said, is changing the game to a \"politics of love.\" \"This win is for every Texan who has ever wondered if anyone is ever listening,\" he said. \"I heard you. We heard you. And tonight, the world hears you.\" Democrat Amy Klobuchar warns that as governor not all may like what she does Klobuchar, who's been in the U.S. Senate for 20 years, said in her victory speech that she's focused on being a \"transformative governor\" for Minnesota. \"I am not interested in moving Minnesota to the left or the right; I want to move us forward,\" she said. She pledged to audit state government and invest in new technology to detect and deter fraud. \"We are going to speed up government, rebuild trust and work for you,\" Klobuchar said. \"Spoiler alert: you may not like every single thing I do.\" Klobuchar also said she was \"not going to be a rubber stamp for Donald Trump. And I will do my job without fear or favor. I will govern for Minnesotans and nobody else.\" 12:47 a.m. EST Trump says he'll accept election results but says 'I don't view it as a hit on me' Trump has congratulated Democrats for their string of victories but maintains that the midterm elections are not a referendum on him. \"The Democrats did a good job. They fought hard,\" he said in a phone interview with Fox News. READ MORE: Trump says Democrats 'did a good job,' blames Republican candidates for midterm losses Several Trump-backed candidates lost in places that he won easily in 2024. But he blamed the candidates themselves, not policies of his that voters have looked on unfavorably, like the economy and Iran war. \"I don't view it as a hit on me,\" he said. \"We've had the greatest two years in the history of the presidency.\" Maine Sen. Susan Collins concedes to Democrat Troy Jackson, ending her run for a sixth term The Associated Press has not yet called the race. Jackson is a former Maine Senate president who took over as the Democratic nominee in July after primary winner Graham Platner dropped out. He was tasked with defeating the longtime incumbent after a chaotic primary season that left the Democrats in disarray and briefly without a candidate. Democrats had seen the race as a top opportunity to flip a Republican-held seat. Maine has supported Democrats for president since 1992, and Collins was running for reelection at a moment when President Trump is deeply unpopular. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, addresses supporters at a watch party during the midterm elections, at the Hilton Garden Inn, in Bangor, Maine, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Taylor Coester/Reuters Iowa Republican Lahn says his loss shows U.S. is at a crossroads Zach Lahn said his defeat to Democrat Rob Sand in the Iowa governor's race sends a message to corporate interests, career politicians and lobbyists. \"America is at a crossroads,\" he said. \"The fight is just beginning right now.\" Lahn called on his supporters to \"protect this state,\" coming after Sand became the first Democrat elected governor in the state in two decades. He said he spoke to Sand and that he'd keep him in his prayers. \"I wish him well in this,\" he said. Democrats flip 3 House seats in Iowa Iowa had an all-Republican congressional delegation going into the election. Democrats have now picked up three of the state's four House seats. In the 1st Congressional District, Christina Bohannan defeated Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks. About 800 votes separated them two years ago, even though Trump comfortably carried the district, setting the stage for Bohannan to win on her third try for the seat. Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott, a state senator and a Lutheran minister, defeated Zach Nunn in the state's 3rd Congressional District. And finally, Democratic candidate Lindsay James, a chaplain, defeated Republican Joe Mitchell in an open seat in the state's 2nd Congressional District. The move by Rep. Ashley Hinson to run for the Senate had left the opening. Both parties invested heavily in a state where farmers are dealing with headwinds from high gas prices and retaliatory tariffs. Democrats flip control of Wisconsin Senate Republican control of the Wisconsin Legislature has come to an end in at least one chamber. Democrats won control of the state Senate on Tuesday and were making gains in the Assembly. Democrats haven't fully controlled Wisconsin's government since 2010. But new legislative districts, ordered by the liberal-controlled Wisconsin Supreme Court, gave Democrats a better shot at flipping the legislative chambers this year. Iowa's Hinson says she'll keep up 'fight for common sense' after defeat Republican Ashley Hinson made brief remarks to supporters after Democrat Josh Turek won Iowa's open seat in the U.S. Senate. Hinson, who serves in the House, was hoping to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Flanked by her family, Hinson thanked her staff and supporters for helping her fight to keep the American dream within reach for more Americans. \"I will continue to fight for common sense,\" Hinson said. \"I think we ran an absolutely fabulous campaign across the state,\" she added. \"Lots of late nights and lots of miles.\" The AP Voter Poll: Hamilton won Kansas Senate voters who were moderates Republican Sen. Roger Marshall performed significantly worse with Kansas Senate voters under 30, with roughly 8 in 10 backing Democrat Adam Hamilton. Marshall split this group with his Democratic opponent in 2020, during his last Senate campaign, according to AP VoteCast. Hamilton won moderates in Kansas this year, with roughly 7 in 10 backing him over Marshall. Marshall only won about one-quarter of this group, down from about 4 in 10 in 2020. Many Kansas voters also appeared concerned about Marshall's character, after he faced accusations throughout the campaign that he had sent unpaid medical bills from former patients to collections agencies. A slim majority of Kansas voters said Marshall did not have the right personal character to serve in the U.S. Senate. About half of voters, by contrast, said Hamilton was \"too extreme.\" 12:27 a.m. EST Gillibrand taken aback by breadth of Democratic Senate wins New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand was confident going into Tuesday but said she was surprised anyway. \"The size of the blue wave is bigger than I ever imagined,\" the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee told The Associated Press. \"It's unbelievable.\" Calling from her hotel after the evening at the committee office watching returns, she at times broke into laughter when ticking through the high points of the evening. For Gillibrand, the biggest thrill was easy. \"Kansas,\" she interrupted. \"First time since 1932.\" Beyond the wins, she credited candidates with talking about issues that were heavy on voters' minds: \"housing costs, fuel costs, medical costs and how they are going to fight for these families across America.\" Democrat Adam Hamilton says win in deeply red Kansas is repudiation of Washington Speaking before a raucous crowd, Hamilton said he won over Republicans and independents because they were not on board with the administration's policies. He cited economic pressure weighing on voters from tariffs along with the war in Iran as factors. \"I think the people in Kansas, Republicans, independents and Democrats are saying what's happening in Washington is not OK,\" he said. He added: \"I got elected because Kansans were saying, 'We're tired of the bullies. We're tired of the chaos,'\" Hamilton said to cheers. Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate from Kansas Adam Hamilton reacts to election results in his hotel suite at a Marriott hotel in Overland Park, Kansas, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Nathan Howard/Reuters Sherrod Brown says Ohio residents 'sent an undeniable message' Democrat Sherrod Brown told supporters they had made themselves clear to the nation. \"You sent an undeniable message tonight: Ohio is not for sale,\" he said. Brown's victory over Republican Sen. Jon Husted was among the most expensive in the nation, topping $500 million in spending by campaigns and outside groups. The former three-term senator pledged to return to Washington to fight for the average Ohio resident. \"My pledge to all Ohioans, whether you voted for me or not, is that I will always be on your side — always,\" he said. Figures wins redrawn Alabama House seat U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures overcame an effort to unseat him through redistricting to win a second term in Alabama's 2nd Congressional District. Figures defeated Trump-backed Republican Rhett Marques. The district had been reshaped to favor the GOP after the U.S. Supreme Court's redistricting decision. \"We had the deck stacked against us,\" Figures said at his victory party. But he said they got to work, \"and we did not look backwards.\" Rob Sand celebrates win in Iowa governor's race Sand told a loud and energized crowd of Democrats in Des Moines that Iowans sent a clear message Tuesday. \"We have to have bigger hearts and minds than just our party,\" Sand said. \"Come January, we will be forced to work together.\" Sand's win breaks a Republican trifecta that's gripped state government for about a decade. He told lawmakers Tuesday that he looks forward to working across the aisle to solve Iowa's problems. Sand also had supporters in the crowd sing an election-night rendition of \"America the Beautiful,\" which he asked attendees to sing at each of his town halls. He also thanked his family and offered a tribute to his late brother-in-law, Walter Lauridsen, who died unexpectedly last month. Democrat Gina Hinojosa says her faith in Texas 'never wavered' in stunning upset The crowd in Austin at her victory party screamed \"Gina\" repeatedly as the Democratic legislator who will be Texas' first Latina governor addressed supporters. \"It never bothered me that they doubted me. It bothered me that they doubted us,\" Hinojosa said. \"Texas, my faith in you never wavered.\" READ MORE: Democrat Gina Hinojosa wins election for governor in Texas Hinojosa said Gov. Abbott had called to congratulate her and offered to assist with her transition into office. Hinojosa is a state lawmaker from Austin who entered the race last year with little money or name recognition. She told supporters about her upbringing along the Texas-Mexico border and her policy priorities, including fighting for public school teachers and keeping billionaires out of politics. \"Your life can be bigger than your dreams,\" she said. Xavier Becerra celebrates Democrats' winning streak in California He'll take over from termed-out Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom. Becerra defeated GOP rival Steve Hilton while campaigning on a promise to push back against Trump and his administration's Republican policies, from immigration to voting rights. READ MORE: Democrat Xavier Becerra wins California governor's race, defeating Republican Steve Hilton \"If anyone wants to come after California or any one Californian, they better be ready for a fight,\" Becerra said at a rally near Sacramento. He'll become the state's first Latino governor since the late 19th century. Becerra was born in Sacramento to a mother from Mexico and a father who was born in California and raised in Mexico. \"What a great night to be an American, to be the son of immigrants from a union household, to be standing in victory with all of you,\" Becerra said. Sen. Chuck Schumer tells voters 'relief is on the way' after Democrats take the Senate The longtime Democratic leader told reporters in Washington that \"Americans voted for change\" and that there had been a \"generational remake of the Senate map.\" \"Five words for the American people: relief is on the way,\" the New York senator said. Texas' Democratic victories a 'rude awakening' After Talarico and Hinojosa won the races for Senate and governor in Texas, respectively, overturning more than three decades of Republican control, voter Aaron Dickerson, 30, said it's a wake-up call for the Lone Star State. \"I think it is a rude awakening,\" said Dickerson, who attended Talarico's exuberant watch party. \"They've been in power here in Texas for 30 years, and I think voters are realizing that, the problems with Texas, the only people to blame are Republicans.\" Trump criticizes Texas governor after loss After Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's defeat, Trump accused him of being a \"RINO,\" or a \"Republican In Name Only.\" Abbott, one of the president's most steadfast allies, lost his bid for a fourth term to Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. \"If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn't become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn't have lost,\" Trump wrote on Truth Social. \"He went back to his original formula, and it wasn't pretty!\" 'Speaker! Speaker!' Cheers erupted for Jeffries after he and his leadership team addressed the crowd at the House Democrats' watch party. Jeffries is in line to make history as the first Black speaker of the House, if Democrats win control and colleagues elect him to the job. 12:05 a.m. EST What to watch at midnight Polls close in Hawaii and almost all of Alaska at midnight. The final polls of the 2026 midterms close at 1 a.m. in the Aleutian Islands, home of Alaska's westernmost polling location. In Alaska in 2024, about 25% of the total vote was not counted on election night. The bulk of the state's mail voting results aren't expected before Nov. 18, the deadline to receive overseas and military ballots. Mail and early in-person ballots comprised about 35% of the total vote in 2022 and about 45% in 2024. Key contests to watch include the Senate and House races in Alaska. Redistricting strategy falters for Republicans Three more Democratic U.S. House members targeted for defeat through redistricting have won reelection. In Alabama, Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures won a second term in a district that was redrawn to help Republicans after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling severely weakened the Voting Rights Act. The Republican redraw dropped the district's Black voting age population from 48% to 40%, making it more challenging for Democrats. While some incumbents affected by redistricting chose to retire or run in another district, Figures viewed the race as still winnable, and both parties ended up investing heavily in the race. Meanwhile, in Texas, Republicans hoped to pick up five seats through redistricting. But Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez won reelection to a sixth term in a reconstituted district that Trump had won by about 10 percentage points over Kamala Harris. And in Ohio, Rep. Greg Landsman, whose district on the westside of Cincinnati was redrawn, won reelection to a third term. Republicans lay blame squarely at Trump's feet Republican campaign officials were unsparing in their blame of President Trump for Tuesday's wholesale losses, particularly in Senate races. The losses in South Carolina, Ohio and Texas — all states Trump carried easily two years ago — were a direct repudiation of the president, two officials with Senate campaigns said. Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot, which they did but not in the way the president hoped, the Republican strategists said, speaking on condition of anonymity to share internal conversations. We can have economic freedom and opportunity, and resist cancel culture and censorship. We can put annus horribilis, 2020, behind us and make America great again, again. We can do all this — if we make the right choice on Nov. 3.\n\nThe New York Post endorses President Donald J. Trump for re-election.\n\n\\*\n\nElections are always about the economy, but never more so than this year.\n\nSo a reminder: Until the necessary shutdown to fight the coronavirus, the unemployment rate stood at 3.5 percent, the lowest in a half-century. African American unemployment was 6.8 percent, the lowest figure since 1972.\n\nAdults out of the workforce for years found new prospects; for 17 months of Trump’s term, there were 1 million more job openings than people unemployed.\n\nThat drove up salaries. For the first time in a decade, wage growth exceeded 3 percent year-over-year. It also narrowed the wealth gap. Between 2016 and 2019, real median incomes rose the most, 9 percent, for those without a high school diploma. Real median incomes declined 2.3 percent for those with a college degree, mostly because older workers retired, according to the Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances.\n\nHow did President Trump do it? First, by trusting the free market. He championed lowering the corporate tax rate to a figure more in line with the rest of the industrialized world. He cut cumbersome regulations, particularly ones rammed through as President Barack Obama was headed out the door. He streamlined the permitting process that would delay infrastructure projects by years, sometimes decades.\n\nA Joe Biden administration would be beholden to a socialist left that sees an opportunity to remake the nation in its vision, one more dependent on government debt. Consider Biden’s dance on fracking — against it for his party, in favor of it in general because he knows what a positive force it’s been for Pennsylvania. Which position would he have in office?\n\nTrump also rejected the globalist axiom that trade deals and unfettered immigration were better for Americans. The US has lost 3.7 million jobs to China since 2001, according to the Economic Policy Institute. And this undermining of our workers with cheap foreign labor did nothing to encourage openness and democracy in Beijing. China’s authoritarianism has only grown worse with concentration camps for Uighurs, crackdowns in Hong Kong and the shuttering of independent churches. The nation remains a manipulative planned economy that devalues its currency and exploits its trade deficit.\n\nFurther, the president recognized that unfettered illegal immigration was unfair to American workers, a common-sense belief held by such right-wingers as Bernie Sanders.\n\nBiden would open the border floodgates again, and by all appearances would go back to “normalization” with China — a byword for them eating our lunch.\n\n\\*\n\nDomestically, President Trump has rolled back the excesses of previous administrations.\n\nHis Education Department reversed Obama’s spectacular overreach that turned college bureaucrats into star-chamber judges in sexual assault cases, with no rights for the accused. He’s encouraged school choice — a work in progress that Biden would stifle because of his fealty to the teachers unions. Trump passed criminal justice reform, freeing those locked up far past the point of reasonable punishment. He rightly railed against the permissiveness of politicians in cities such as Portland to the lawlessness on their streets.\n\nHe’s defended pride in American values against those who slander our entire nation as a racist enterprise.\n\nMost importantly, throughout his time in office and culminating with the nomination of Amy Coney Barrett, Trump’s judicial appointments promise to curb the leftward shift of the courts and the activism that Democrats have come to count on. The left has achieved through legal decisions what it couldn’t through legislation.\n\nA new crop of judges and justices promises to decide the law on its constitutionality, not through activism.\n\n\\*\n\nJoe Biden has tried to make this election about the coronavirus, but it’s unclear he’d do anything different except trigger new lockdowns — a strategy the WHO now discourages.\n\nTrump is criticized for his early handling of the virus, but his institution of a travel ban and aid to the states undoubtedly saved lives. The same perfect hindsight the media expects of the president they rarely apply to others. Consider that Gov. Andrew Cuomo wrote a self-praising book about his response to COVID-19, even though New York’s death toll is higher than that of any other state. And because he’s a Democrat, the media let him get away with it!\n\nToday, those who are infected with the coronavirus survive at much higher rates. We are likely to have a vaccine in the coming months, far earlier than many experts thought possible. The media don’t want to admit it, but that’s all thanks to the “warp speed” policy instituted by the White House.\n\n\\*\n\nOn foreign policy, President Trump has repeatedly embarrassed the conventional wisdom. After previous administrations promised but did not move our embassy to Jerusalem, he did so, and, despite the doomsayers, nothing happened.\n\nThe Obama administration tried to co-opt Iran with bundles of cash, which the theocratic regime used to sow chaos across the region, stirring up unrest in Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen and the West Bank. The Trump administration cut off the money, killed the architect of the terror campaign, Qasem Soleimani, and, despite the doomsayers, the world became safer. The result? Arab nations have increasingly accepted Israel, signing historic peace deals.\n\nAs promised, Trump has not entangled us in new foreign wars, and has been pulling us out of the old ones. He cajoled Mexico to handle immigration caravans from Central America, and successfully pushed NATO allies to pay more of their commitments. When journalists write that the United States has “lost its standing in the world,” they usually mean our standing at Davos cocktail parties. For the rest of us, it’s clear that Trumpism is focused on pursuing what’s best for our country.\n\n\\*\n\nHere’s the part about Twitter. This paper has, before the 2016 election and often through his term, bemoaned President Trump’s habit of speaking before he thinks.
